summary: Describes NETBUGGER3, a third-level program from UCLA for debugging network programs and trying out protocols. The authors needed a stand-in for a remote system that would not be up for months, and realized many sites had the same problem.

plainLanguage.summary: A pretend friend you can practice with. When the real computer is not ready, this program acts like it so you can test your own.

questions: how to test network protocols in 1971
how did early networks test protocols
subtitle: A tool for testing network protocols when the remote system is not yet operational.

tldr.problem: Network researchers needed to test and debug new protocols, but the remote systems they were building to talk to were not available for weeks or months.
tldr.mechanism: NETBUGGER3 is a program running at UCLA-NMC that simulates a remote network service, accepting connection requests, responding to protocol messages, and allowing engineers to view and manipulate data flowing between systems.
tldr.outcome: Teams could test their protocols against a working simulator instead of waiting for actual hardware to be deployed, and other sites could arrange to use NETBUGGER3 for their own testing.

today: NETBUGGER3 is a historical artifact showing how early network researchers addressed testing challenges. Modern protocol development uses simulation frameworks, mock servers and network emulation to test without operational remote systems.

sections.title: The Problem and the Tool
sections.content:
The UCLA Network Measurement Center faced a familiar problem: they were writing an RJE (remote job entry) FILENET protocol to interact with UCLA-CCN, but that system would not be operational for several months. They needed a program that could simulate CCN so they could test their protocol without waiting.

Mark Kampe realized that many sites on the network had the same problem: they could not debug client programs because the intended server was not yet running. So he started writing NETBUGGER3, a third-level debugger and simulator that could stand in for any remote system.
sections.plainLanguage: A group at UCLA was building a program to talk to a computer that would not be ready for months. They wrote NETBUGGER3 to pretend to be that computer, so they could test their code right away.

sections.title: What NETBUGGER3 Can Do
sections.content:
NETBUGGER3 runs at UCLA-NMC and lets a user issue Network Control Program (NCP) commands like RTS (request to send), STR (start transmit request) and LISTEN. The user can check the status of connections, receive and display NCP-USER events, and exchange data over up to twelve simultaneous connections.

Received data can be displayed in ASCII, EBCDIC or hexadecimal. The user can originate data for transmission in the same formats. NETBUGGER3 can act as the initiator, receiver or intermediate in network connections, making it flexible enough to simulate a wide range of protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: NETBUGGER3 lets someone send and receive messages, open and close connections, and see exactly what data is flowing. A person at UCLA can watch and control what the pretend server does.

sections.title: How Other Sites Used It
sections.content:
Other hosts on the network could arrange with UCLA to test their protocols against NETBUGGER3. Alternatively, a host could use Telnet to log into the UCLA system and start NETBUGGER3 themselves, running it on one console while testing their protocol implementation on another.

Later, when the actual remote server became operational, NETBUGGER3 could be used as an intermediate proxy between the client and server, allowing engineers to monitor and debug the real communication by viewing and editing messages as they passed through.
sections.plainLanguage: People from other computers could call UCLA over the network and start NETBUGGER3 to test their protocol. Or later, NETBUGGER3 could sit between the real computers and let someone see what they are saying to each other.
